summary.title: Broad Phase Collision Detection Using Spatial Partitioning
summary.one_liner: You learn how broad-phase collision detection works by comparing brute-force pair testing with a simple spatial grid that buckets AABBs into square cells and tests only entities that share a cell.
keywords: how to detect collisions between many game objects
how to speed up collision detection in games
takeaways: Broad phase quickly finds object pairs that might collide; narrow phase then checks exact collisions.
Brute force pair testing is simple but its cost grows quadratically with entity count.
A spatial grid maps AABBs to square cells, rebuilt each update, and only tests entities sharing a cell.
Cell size must be tuned to entity size; mixed-size entities make a simple grid degrade toward brute force.
Caching checked pairs by unique entity IDs avoids duplicate tests.
summary.summary: The article explains broad-phase collision detection in game development and compares two approaches: a brute-force nested loop over entity pairs, and a simple spatial grid. It uses JavaScript demos built on a custom engine (the ro namespace) with axis-aligned bounding boxes defined by min and max points, and it sandboxes demos in JSFiddle. The grid section covers cell mapping formulas, cell-size trade-offs, grid population each step, and querying pairs with an ID-based cache to avoid duplicate tests. It closes with limitations for entities of varying size and ideas for extensions, plus a worked example comparing collision check counts.
